fatal_flaws.claim: "Idempotency comes free from the instance id: `gen:{siteId}:{intakeHash}` — Workflows rejects a duplicate instance id... This makes the `locked_by`/`lock_expires_at` cooperative lease in `generation_jobs` redundant."
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: Three independent defects. (1) The ID is syntactically invalid: Cloudflare's Workers API doc requires instance IDs to match `^[a-zA-Z0-9_][a-zA-Z0-9-_]*$` — colons are not in that class, so every `create()` call fails on the very first generation. (2) `create()` throws if the ID belongs to any existing instance that has not passed its retention limit, and retention on Workers Paid is 30 days. A terminally failed job (refusal → `needs_review`, or exhausted retries during an Anthropic outage) therefore locks that exact intake out of regeneration for 30 days — the user resubmits the identical form, gets the same `intakeHash`, and is permanently blocked. (3) Cloudflare's own Rules of Workflows says the opposite of this design: "Instance ID Uniqueness: Use unique identifiers per invocation. Reusing IDs prevents tracking multiple instances for the same user." The design then instructs the parent agent to retire the working `locked_by` lease in favour of this.
fatal_flaws.correction: Keep the instance ID unique per invocation (`gen_{runId}`, sanitised to `[A-Za-z0-9_-]`, ≤100 chars — note `gen:{30-char siteId}:{64-char sha}` is 99 chars with zero headroom anyway). Enforce idempotency where it already works: `generation_jobs.idempotency_key` with its existing `uq_jobs_idem` unique index, plus the HTTP `Idempotency-Key` + `prompt_sha256` 409 check the design already specifies in §7.5 layer 1. Keep the `locked_by`/`lock_expires_at` lease and `idx_jobs_reaper`. If you want infrastructure-level dedupe, `createBatch()` is documented as idempotent (existing in-retention IDs are skipped rather than throwing) — but it does not solve the 30-day lockout either.

fatal_flaws.claim: "One frozen mega-prefix shared by *every* call type... One identical 50K prefix for all ten calls... buys a single always-warm entry with a near-100% hit rate." Cost table then varies `effort` per call: high, high, medium×5, medium×2, low.
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: Varying `effort` is exactly what breaks the shared cache. The Anthropic caching reference's invalidation hierarchy lists `thinking` or `effort` change as: messages cache **not** preserved, tools/system cache **model-specific**. The prose is explicit: "Thinking and `effort` changes always invalidate the messages cache, and on models that render the thinking configuration ahead of tools and system they invalidate those caches too — pin thinking and effort settings per route rather than varying them per request." BP2 (the ~1.8K business-facts block, which lives in `messages`) is guaranteed dead on every effort change. Whether the 48K BP1 system block survives on `claude-opus-5` is undocumented — and the design bets its entire $2.24/site caching saving on the favourable answer without a single sentence acknowledging the risk. Worst case you get three cache namespaces (high/medium/low), three cold writes, and the "caching is worth ~49% of the job" claim collapses.
fatal_flaws.correction: The fix is documented and available on this exact model: per-message effort via beta `mid-conversation-output-config-2026-07-01` (Claude Opus 5, Claude API) — a `{"role":"system", "content": [], "output_config": {"effort": ...}}` message changes effort "without the messages-cache invalidation that a top-level `effort` change causes," and is exempt from the usual placement rules. Pin top-level `effort` to one value for all ten calls and modulate per call with that message. Then verify empirically with `usage.cache_read_input_tokens` before trusting any number in §2 — that field is the only ground truth.

fatal_flaws.claim: The entire §2 cost model. Output column: 6,000 / 9,000 / 9,500×5 / 4,000×2 / 800 = 71,300 tokens → $1.783.
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: There is no line for thinking tokens anywhere in the design, and thinking is billed as output. On `claude-opus-5` adaptive thinking is **on by default** (unlike Opus 4.8/4.7, where omitting `thinking` runs without it), and `display` controls visibility only — "thinking happens and is billed the same under every setting." `plan-brief` is a high-effort, compounding-design-judgment call over a 48K prefix; its thinking is plausibly comparable to or larger than its 6K structured output. The schema author already knew this: `generation_jobs.thinking_tokens` exists in `0005_ai_generation.sql`, and the design's own proposed `generation_calls` table silently drops it. Two knock-on errors compound this: (a) `ttl:"1h"` cache writes cost **2×** base, not 1.25× — the doc is explicit ("Cache writes cost 1.25× for 5-minute TTL, 2× for 1-hour TTL") — so the prefix write is $10/MTok = **$0.48**, not $0.30, and the "≤$7.20/day" floor is ≤$11.52/day per distinct prefix; (b) the cache-read total is arithmetically wrong: 48,000 + 9×49,800 = **496,200**, not 516,200.
fatal_flaws.correction: Add a `thinking_tokens` column to `generation_calls` (mirroring `generation_jobs`), and treat COGS as unknown until measured — plan for $3.50–4.50 per 6-locale site, not $2.30, and re-derive the "11% of revenue" claim from real `usage` data. Also correct the write premium to 2× and re-check whether 1h TTL earns it: the doc notes a cache read refreshes the entry's timer for free, so "requests that share a prefix and start less than 5 minutes apart keep the 5-minute cache warm indefinitely — the 1-hour TTL buys nothing there except the doubled write price." The design itself observes this and then picks 1h anyway. (The one legitimate reason to keep 1h: the doc says a `max_tokens: 0` keep-alive is rejected with structured outputs, so "use the 1-hour TTL instead" — state that as the reason.)

fatal_flaws.claim: "Pexels is the sole automatic stock source. Unsplash is disabled for generated sites." Pipeline: "fetch top 12 candidates" per query, code-composed queries for hero + sections + 2 blog featured images.
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: Pexels API keys carry a default rate limit of **200 requests/hour and 20,000 requests/month**. Neither number appears anywhere in the design. At even one search call per site you are capped at 20,000 sites/month; at a realistic 6–10 calls per site (hero video, hero poster, about, services tiles, gallery, 2 blog heroes) you get roughly 2,000–3,000 sites/month and **~20–30 sites/hour**. The 200/hour ceiling is the binding one: it throttles signup throughput to a rate a single marketing push would saturate, and it is a hard third-party limit on the critical path of the free onboarding generation. Having architecturally disqualified Unsplash, the design has no fallback — this is a single point of failure with a documented, low, undiscussed ceiling.
fatal_flaws.correction: Apply for the free unlimited-limit upgrade before launch (Pexels grants it, but requires eligibility review and a demonstrated attribution implementation — so build the credit line first and budget calendar time). Independently: cache search results by composed-query hash in R2/KV so the 300-pizzeria case costs one API call not 300 (the design already content-addresses the *downloads*, but not the *queries*); pre-seed a curated per-industry pool so a Pexels outage or 429 degrades to a stock library rather than failing the job; and make `resolve-media` degrade to poster-only/no-media rather than failing the step.

fatal_flaws.claim: The whole persistence design assumes one D1 database. §7.4 atomic publish writes a full staging `site_versions` tree per generation; §7.7 allows 10 regenerations/tenant/month; the design adds `generation_calls` (10 rows/job) and `page_slug_aliases` that "serves 301s forever."
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: A single D1 database holds a maximum of **10 GB on Workers Paid, and that limit cannot be raised — not on request, not on Enterprise**. Cloudflare's own D1 docs state the product is "designed for horizontal scale out across multiple, smaller (10 GB) databases, such as per-user, per-tenant or per-entity databases." Do the arithmetic on this schema: `pages` and `page_translations` are both version-scoped (`site_version_id NOT NULL`), so every regeneration inserts a complete fresh set — 8 pages × 6 locales = 48 `page_translations` rows per version, each carrying `jsonld` (≤16 KB inline), `title`, `meta_description`, `path`, and possibly `content_inline` (≤64 KB inline), across five indexes. At 10,000 tenants × 11 versions/month that is ~5.3M rows/month; even with all page trees pushed to R2 and only a 1–2 KB LocalBusiness graph per row, you cross 10 GB within weeks. Nothing in the design prunes old versions, and `page_slug_aliases` is explicitly unbounded.
fatal_flaws.correction: Decide the sharding story now, before any query is written — it is the one-way door in this design. Either per-tenant D1 databases (Cloudflare's stated pattern, and it makes the 10 GB cap a non-issue forever) or a hard version-retention policy (keep N versions + the live one, GC the rest) plus moving `jsonld` and all page content to R2 behind `content_sha256`. Cross-tenant reporting queries (`idx_jobs_org_cost`, the cost rollup) need to be designed against whichever you pick — retrofitting sharding after the API layer exists means rewriting every data access path.

fatal_flaws.claim: The Workflow's `emit()` helper — `await emit("api_call", 15)`, `emit("streaming", 45)`, `emit("build", 80)`, `emit("done", 100)` — calls `hub.fetch(...)` directly in `run()`, outside any `step.do()`.
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: Cloudflare's Rules of Workflows: "Side Effects Outside Steps: Logic with side effects outside `step.do()` may execute multiple times due to engine restarts" and "Do not store state outside of a step." `run()` is replayed on every resume, so each retry of a fan-out step re-fires every prior `emit()` — duplicating rows in the DO's append-only SQL log, re-emitting SSE events, and making the progress bar jump backwards. That directly damages the one thing the design says the DO exists for: the narrated "magic popup" UX. The append-only log with `Last-Event-ID` resume makes this worse, not better — replayed events get new sequence numbers and clients cannot dedupe them.
fatal_flaws.correction: Move every emit inside its adjacent `step.do()` (returning the emitted event as part of the step result so replay is memoised), or make the DO's `/emit` endpoint idempotent on a deterministic key (`{runId}:{phase}` or the step name) with `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`. The design already applies exactly this discipline to `generation_calls` via `uq_calls_step`; apply it to the event log too.

fatal_flaws.claim: "The tenant CSP then becomes shippable: `default-src 'none'; img-src 'self' data:; media-src 'self'; style-src 'unsafe-inline'; script-src 'sha256-…'; base-uri 'none'; form-action 'self'` — itself a Lighthouse best-practices signal."
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: As written this policy breaks the site the design describes. (a) `connect-src` is absent and falls back to `default-src 'none'`, so the "deferred 400-byte beacon" in §6 item 6 is blocked outright — as is any `fetch`/`sendBeacon`. (b) `img-src 'self'` blocks images, because §6 serves them through "Cloudflare Images transformations in front of the R2 bucket via a custom domain" — a different origin from `<slug>.mijnsaas.com`. (c) `script-src 'sha256-…'` covers inline scripts, but §6 item 6 specifies "one `defer`red file", which needs `'self'`. (d) `frame-ancestors` does **not** fall back to `default-src`, so every tenant site is freely framable. Separately, the claim that CSP is a Lighthouse scoring signal is wrong: the `csp-xss` audit is informative/zero-weight and does not move the Best Practices score.
fatal_flaws.correction: `default-src 'none'; script-src 'self'; style-src 'unsafe-inline'; img-src 'self' data:; media-src 'self'; font-src 'self'; connect-src 'self'; form-action 'self'; base-uri 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'` — and resolve (b) by deciding the image origin question below before writing it.

fatal_flaws.claim: §6 states an R2 layout of pre-generated derivatives (`img/{sha256}/{w}.avif|.webp|.jpg`, w ∈ {400…2400}), preloads them as same-origin paths (`/img/ab12/800.avif`), AND says "Cloudflare Images transformations in front of the R2 bucket via a custom domain" because "a Worker cannot encode AVIF at any sane CPU cost" — while §6's headline perf rule is "Zero third-party origins."
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: These cannot all be true. If transformations are on-the-fly via an Images custom domain, the `/img/{sha}/{w}.avif` R2 objects never exist, the preload URLs are fiction, that domain is a cross-origin DNS+TLS handshake on the LCP path, and it violates both `img-src 'self'` and "zero third-party origins" — the exact charge levelled at Unsplash to disqualify it. If the derivatives are genuinely pre-generated and stored in R2, then something must encode 15 variants per image and the design names no encoder (Containers appear only in Phase 3, for video). There is also a cost error either way: Cloudflare Images transformations are billed per unique image+option combination **once a month, recurring** — at 5 widths × 3 formats × ~12 images per site that is ~180 unique transformations per site *per month*, ~$900/month at 10,000 tenants ($0.50/1,000, 5,000 free), not the one-time cost the "bounds the billable transformation set" phrasing implies.
fatal_flaws.correction: Pick one. Cleanest for the 100/100 target: pre-generate the ladder once in a Container/ffmpeg-or-libavif step at `resolve-media` time, store in R2, serve **same-origin** through the site Worker at `/img/...` with `immutable` caching. That keeps `img-src 'self'`, keeps zero third-party origins, and turns a recurring per-month transformation bill into a one-time encode plus R2 storage. If you keep Images transforms, drop the "zero third-party origins" claim and model the recurring monthly cost honestly.

fatal_flaws.claim: "Sections carry zero prose. They carry SLOT IDS. Code derives the slot inventory from the section list; **the model cannot invent a slot id**." — while the wire schema has the model emit `headlineSlot: z.string()`, `subheadSlot`, `bodySlots: z.array(z.string())`, `titleSlot`, `descriptionSlot`, etc.
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: Self-contradictory, and the contradiction is load-bearing. If code derives slot ids from `(sectionId, field, index)`, those `*Slot` string fields are redundant and are precisely a channel for the model to emit an id that disagrees with the derived one. If the model authors them, then it *can* invent slot ids and `deriveSlotInventory(struct)` cannot be a pure function over the section list — it is just reading back what the model wrote, so `validateBundle` is comparing model output against model output and proves nothing about coverage. §5's "adding a 7th language is one INSERT… no slot id change" rests on the derived reading; the schema implements the authored one.
fatal_flaws.correction: Delete every `*Slot: z.string()` field from the wire schema. Slot ids become `${section.id}.headline`, `${section.id}.items.${i}.title`, `${page.pageId}.meta.title` — derived identically by the renderer, the editor, `deriveSlotInventory`, and the translation validator. This also shrinks the structure document and removes a whole class of referential-integrity repair.

fatal_flaws.claim: "Every link is a symbolic ref… `{kind:"external",refId}` where `refId` indexes a server-built allowlist (GBP URL + socials from onboarding). Kills `javascript:`, phishing, and SSRF." And: "a *fully successful* prompt injection yields nothing exploitable — the worst case is bad copy."
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: The allowlist is built from the onboarding form, which §7.8 correctly identifies as attacker-controlled. An allowlist populated by the attacker is not an allowlist against that attacker. It kills `javascript:` (if you scheme-validate, which the design never states) and SSRF from *model-invented* URLs, but it does nothing against phishing: sign up, put your phishing URL in the socials field, get a Claude-written, Lighthouse-perfect, valid-TLS page on `*.mijnsaas.com` linking to it. "Worst case is bad copy" also understates the real threat — bad copy on a live public site under your own brand's apex domain *is* the attack (scam offers, defamation, fake medical claims), and the only control named for it is a single "moderation pass on assembled copy before publish" with no specification.
fatal_flaws.correction: State the scheme allowlist explicitly (`https:` only, plus `tel:`/`mailto:` built by code). Validate every onboarding-supplied external URL against a phishing/brand blocklist and a domain-age/reputation check at intake — the design already does exactly this for custom hostnames in §7.8 and should reuse it. Specify the pre-publish moderation pass (model, prompt, what it blocks, what happens on a hit) rather than naming it. And reframe the §1 claim: the output contract defeats *code injection*, not *content abuse*; the latter needs the intake screen and moderation, which is a detection problem with a false-negative rate.

fatal_flaws.claim: "CI guarantee: a Playwright matrix renders every `(preset × variant × section-type × locale-with-longest-strings)` combination and asserts… A preset that fails cannot ship. This is why the model 'can't invent broken CSS' — the space it selects from is pre-proven."
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: Not executable at the stated scope. §4 computes 24 presets × 3 palette variants × 5 hue shifts × 4 radii × 3 densities ≈ 4,320 reachable looks. Crossed with 17 section types and 6 locales that is ~440,000 browser renders per CI run; even collapsing to preset×variant×section it is 73,440 screenshots. This is the single claim the entire §4 "the model selects from a pre-proven space" argument depends on, and it cannot run on any CI budget. The knobs also do not decompose cleanly: `accentHueShift` (±30° OKLCH) interacts with `paletteVariant` and `colorMode` on contrast, and `densityId` interacts with locale string length on overflow — so you cannot factorise the matrix into independent axes and call it covered.
fatal_flaws.correction: Split the guarantee by what each check actually needs. Contrast is analytic — compute the full 4,320-look token contrast matrix in pure code with zero browsers, on every commit, and make unreadable pairs unrepresentable as claimed. Overflow, tap-target and CLS need rendering: cover them with a fixed representative sample (24 presets × 3 variants × 17 sections × the single longest-string locale ≈ 1,200 renders — tractable) plus a nightly randomised sweep over the remaining knob space. Then state the guarantee honestly: contrast is proven, layout is sampled.

fatal_flaws.claim: "Not Queues, not DO alarms. Both cap at 15 min wall clock… Workflows has **no wall-clock cap per step**."
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: Half right, and the wrong half is the one the argument rests on. The Workflows limits table does say "Duration (wall clock) per step: Unlimited" — but Rules of Workflows states "Step timeouts must be 30 minutes maximum; use `step.waitForEvent()` for longer waits," and the `StepConfig` timeout defaults to 10 minutes. So the real comparison is 15 min (Queues) vs 30 min (Workflows step), not 15 min vs unbounded. The conclusion still holds — Workflows is the right primitive, and per-step memoisation is the real reason — but the margin is 2×, not infinite, and a step whose config omits `timeout` (the design's `RETRY` constant, used for `copy-primary`, all five `localize`, both `blog`, and `legal-variables`) silently inherits the 10-minute default, which is *tighter* than the 10-minute SDK timeout the design sets on `plan-brief`.
fatal_flaws.correction: State the 30-minute ceiling. Set an explicit `timeout` on every `step.do` rather than relying on the 10-minute default, and keep each step's SDK `timeout` strictly below its step `timeout` so the SDK aborts first and produces a typed error the retry ladder can classify — otherwise the step timeout fires and you lose the transport-vs-content distinction §7.6 is built on.

fatal_flaws.claim: "So the schema is **two-layer**: `wire.ts` — constraint-free, model-facing… `domain.ts` — the same shapes `.extend()`ed with `.min()`/`.max()`/`.regex()`/`.refine()`, applied **after** parse." Justified by: Structured Outputs rejects `minLength`/`maxLength`/`minimum`/`maximum`.
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: The premise about the subset is correct, but the conclusion does not follow for this SDK. The structured-outputs documentation states: "The Python and TypeScript SDKs automatically handle unsupported constraints by removing them from the schema sent to the API and validating them client-side." You are on `@anthropic-ai/sdk`. So a single Zod schema carrying `.min()`/`.max()` passed to `zodOutputFormat()` already does exactly what the two-layer split does by hand. The split therefore buys nothing for its stated reason while creating a permanent drift hazard — two definitions of 17 section types that must stay structurally identical forever, with `Page`/`StrictPage`-style divergence already visible in the sketch. It also motivates encoding every bounded numeric as a string enum (`Count`, `Shift`), which pushes `Number()` casts into the renderer, the design system and the editor permanently — and `schemaVersion: "1"` is stamped into all three stored document types, so reversing it later is a versioned migration of R2 blobs.
fatal_flaws.correction: Keep one schema per document with real constraints, pass it to `zodOutputFormat()`, and let the SDK strip-and-validate. Keep the design's genuinely good rules — every field required + `.nullable()` never `.optional()`, no recursion, `additionalProperties: false` — and keep a separate *cross-document* referential-integrity pass (`validateBundle`, media/link refs), which is real work Zod cannot do. Two notes in the design's favour: `anyOf` and `$ref`/`$defs` *are* supported, so the discriminated unions are fine; and the 24h grammar-compilation cache claim is correct.

fatal_flaws.claim: §7.7 allowance table: `trialing`/`active` gets "1 regeneration / 24h, 10 / month; soft cap **$8 model spend / tenant / month**" — alongside "€9,99/mo billed annually ≈ €119,88 ≈ $130/yr" and "~$14.5/yr COGS ≈ 11% of revenue."
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: Internally inconsistent by a wide margin, in the section that exists to protect margin. 10 regenerations/month at the design's own $2.30 each is $23/month — nearly 3× the $8 soft cap and more than double gross monthly revenue. The $8 cap itself is 74% of the ~$10.83/month the annual plan yields. The revenue figure is also gross: €9,99 to an EU consumer is normally VAT-inclusive (21% NL → €8.26 net), and Stripe takes ~1.5% + €0.25 on EU cards, so realistic net is closer to €98/yr ≈ $107. With thinking tokens folded in (flaw 3), COGS is plausibly 25–35% of net revenue, not 11%.
fatal_flaws.correction: Derive the caps from net revenue and measured COGS, not the other way round: pick a target COGS fraction (say 20% of net ≈ $21/yr), divide by measured cost per completed site, and set the monthly regeneration cap to that number — likely 4–6/month, not 10. Make the $ cap and the count cap consistent so one is redundant. Price the trial generation separately since it converts at well under 100%.

fatal_flaws.claim: `https://<slug>.mijnsaas.com/` → "302 by Accept-Language (`Vary: Accept-Language`)", with `x-default` pointing at that root.
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: Two costs the design does not weigh. (1) `Vary: Accept-Language` on the apex makes the most-shared, most-linked URL of every tenant site effectively uncacheable at the edge (the header has near-unbounded cardinality), and adds a redirect round-trip to LCP on exactly the URL a small business prints on a flyer — in a section whose thesis is that third-party DNS+TLS handshakes are unacceptable on the LCP path. (2) Googlebot crawls predominantly from US IPs and does not send a meaningful `Accept-Language`, so `x-default` resolves to `/en/` for the crawler on a Dutch bakery's site.
fatal_flaws.correction: Serve the primary locale's content at `/` directly (200, no redirect, `Vary` omitted, canonical → `/nl/`), and do language selection client-side with a dismissible banner rather than a server redirect. Point `x-default` at `/` and let it be a real page. If you keep the redirect, use 302 + `Cache-Control: private` deliberately and accept the cache loss with eyes open.

fatal_flaws.claim: "Fonts are self-hosted, always. **Eight curated variable-font pairings**, subset to latin + latin-ext… self-hosted `woff2` variable subsets."
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: The §4 table names ~21 distinct families across 20 rows (Space Grotesk, Playfair Display, Source Sans 3, Fraunces, Cormorant, Karla, Tenor Sans, Marcellus, Nunito Sans, Oswald, Inter Tight, Instrument Sans, Lora, Barlow Condensed, Archivo, Libre Caslon, Anton, Cinzel, Poppins, Cormorant Garamond, Barlow) — not eight pairings. Several have no variable-font release (Tenor Sans, Marcellus, Anton, Libre Caslon Text, Cormorant), so "variable subsets" is not achievable for them, and each static weight is a separate file against the perf budget. Row 8 lists "Söhne-alt (Inter Tight)" — Söhne is a commercially licensed typeface; naming it even as an alias in a shipping design system is a licensing hazard worth removing.
fatal_flaws.correction: Reconcile the count, verify variable availability per family before committing the preset table (it is baked into `industries.design_preset` JSON), and drop the Söhne reference. The self-hosting rationale itself is correct and well argued — the German Google Fonts / GDPR exposure is real and it is a genuine differentiator for this market.

fatal_flaws.claim: "Workers AI safety/content classification" as a pipeline step over Pexels candidate images; and "1 free generation per verified email and per IP /24 per day."
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: (a) The Workers AI catalogue has no first-class image-safety/NSFW classifier — Llama Guard 3 is text-only, and the vision models (LLaVA and similar) are captioning/VLM models, not moderation classifiers. Treating this as a solved step understates the work and the per-image latency/cost of a VLM call on 12 candidates per site. (b) `/24` is IPv4-only reasoning: most European mobile traffic is IPv6 (where the meaningful unit is /64 or /48) and much of the rest is behind CGNAT, where a /24 daily cap will block legitimate signups from a whole ISP pool.
fatal_flaws.correction: Name a concrete moderation approach for images (a VLM prompt with an explicit rubric, or a third-party moderation API, with measured cost) rather than a capability. For rate limiting, key on verified email + Turnstile + Stripe payment method (the design already requires all three for regeneration) and treat IP as a weak secondary signal with separate IPv4 /24 and IPv6 /48 buckets.

missing: **GDPR posture for the AI pipeline itself.** The design argues against Google Fonts on GDPR grounds and against Unsplash on "transfers every visitor's IP to a US CDN" grounds — then ships every tenant's business data, uploaded photos (possibly containing identifiable people), and free-text description to a US LLM provider with no mention of a DPA, Art. 28 subprocessor disclosure, retention terms, or `inference_geo` (a real top-level Messages API parameter that pins where inference runs). The product also *auto-generates each tenant's Privacy Policy*, which must name the tenant's own subprocessors — so this gap propagates into a legal document you are producing on their behalf. This is the single most inconsistent thing in the document given its stated market.

**Any evaluation of output quality.** There is no eval set, no golden-output regression, no human rubric — nothing that measures whether the generated site is *good*, which is the entire product. Meanwhile §2 says system block 5 churns "weekly" and blocks 3/4/8 churn "monthly." Every one of those edits silently rewrites the 48K cached prefix (paying a fresh 2× write) and silently changes design and copy quality for every subsequent tenant, with no way to detect a regression. Build a fixed intake set (~30 businesses across verticals and locales), score structure/design/copy/SEO, and gate prompt-block changes on it.

**Incremental re-translation.** The design treats translation as a one-shot fan-out from the primary bundle. It never says what happens when the user edits one string in the live editor: the other five locales are now wrong. `page_translations.is_stale` and `idx_page_tr_stale` already exist in `0004_pages_content.sql` — the schema author anticipated this and the design does not use it. At 6 locales this is the dominant ongoing cost and correctness problem, and the flat `entries[]` shape makes a cheap per-slot re-translation call entirely feasible.

**Blog locale coverage.** Calls 8–9 generate two posts in the primary locale only, but `blog_index` is a page role and `blog_teaser` is a section type available in all six locales. So `/de/blog/` is either empty (thin-content SEO penalty on a page you emit hreflang for) or shows Dutch posts. `blog_post_translations` exists in the schema and is never referenced. Decide: translate the posts, or omit the blog from non-primary locales and drop it from the hreflang set and sitemap.

**Where `reviews` data comes from.** The `reviews` section is selectable on every site with `source: "google" | "manual" | "mixed"` and a `google_badge` variant, but onboarding collects only a GBP *URL* — which yields no review data. Google Places API returns at most 5 reviews with display restrictions, and scraping is against ToS. `site_reviews` exists in `0004`. Either wire a real source with its licensing constraints, or restrict the enum to `manual` and design the collection flow.

**`booking` with `provider: "native"` / `variant: "inline_calendar"` versus the 4 KB JS budget.** §6 enumerates the entire JS payload — "WhatsApp button, mobile nav, video swap, banner, form" — with no calendar, no availability fetch, no timezone handling. An inline booking calendar is not deliverable inside that budget. Either drop `native`/`inline_calendar` from the wire enum for Phase 1–2 or state which budget it breaks and by how much.

**Cancellation.** The state machine includes `cancelled` and the DO owns run-level truth, but nothing calls the Workflows instance `terminate()`. Without it a cancelled job keeps burning Anthropic tokens through the fan-out — the most expensive part — while the UI shows it stopped.

**Whether the `AnthropicLimiter` global DO is needed, or is itself the bottleneck.** A single DO is single-threaded and pinned to one colo, so every one of the ~10 calls per job pays a cross-region round trip to it, and a ~20-in-flight global bucket caps throughput at roughly 1–2 sites/minute account-wide — which does not survive 10,000 tenants. It also has no stated lease/TTL, so a Worker that dies holding a token leaks capacity permanently. Worth noting the design may be over-engineering against a partly-relieved risk: on the Claude API, cache reads do not count toward input-token rate limits on most models, and ~49.8K of each ~50K-token request is a cache read.

**Slug persistence across versions.** §5 says "On first publish, the resolved slug is written to `page_translations` and never regenerated" — but `pages` and `page_translations` are both version-scoped with fresh ids per generation, so "the stored slug wins" requires an explicit lookup into the previously *published* version keyed by `page_key` + `locale`. That lookup, and what happens when a regeneration drops a page entirely (does its slug 301 to the home page, or 410?), is unspecified. The 301-alias idea is right; the mechanism needs to name `pages.page_key` as the join key.
verdict: Roughly two-thirds of this is genuinely strong, and I want to be clear about which two-thirds because the good parts are unusually good. The §1 hybrid output contract is the correct call and the reasoning for it is right: making the model emit selections and prose while code owns every rendered byte is the only design that survives a hostile signup, and the four invariants are the right four. The Unsplash analysis is excellent and correctly reasoned from licence terms to architecture (mandatory hotlinking → third-party origin on the LCP path → incompatible; plus no video API). Content-addressed R2 with a fixed width ladder, atomic publish via a staging `site_versions` row, per-step memoisation as the reason to choose Workflows, `maxRetries: 0` so Workflows owns retries, separating transport from content failures in the retry ladder, deterministic repair before model repair, and the OKLCH-derived token system are all correct and well argued. On the API facts specifically the design is more accurate than most: `server-side-fallback-2026-07-01` + `fallbacks: "default"` is real, `stop_details.category` is real and only populated on refusal, `max_tokens: 0` really is rejected alongside `output_config.format`, `response.parsed_output` really is the TS field and really can be null, the 4-breakpoint limit and the 24-hour grammar cache are right, `anyOf`/`$defs` really are supported so the discriminated unions are fine, `Promise.all` over `step.do` really is permitted (only `Promise.race`/`Promise.any` must be wrapped), and the Cloudflare Workers CPU/subrequest/Queues/DO-alarm/Cloudflare-for-SaaS numbers all check out against current docs. That is a lot of verified homework. But three things are load-bearing and broken. The Workflow instance ID `gen:{siteId}:{intakeHash}` cannot be created at all — colons violate the documented `^[a-zA-Z0-9_][a-zA-Z0-9-_]*$` pattern — and even once sanitised it converts any terminal failure into a 30-day regeneration lockout for that tenant, while the design instructs the parent agent to delete the `locked_by` lease that actually works. Varying `effort` across the ten calls destroys the single shared cache prefix that the entire cost model is built on ("pin thinking and effort settings per route rather than varying them per request"), and the fix — per-message effort via `mid-conversation-output-config-2026-07-01`, available on exactly this model — is documented and unused. And the cost model has no line for thinking tokens at all, on a model where adaptive thinking is on by default and billed as output, so $2.30/site and "11% of revenue" are not numbers anyone should plan against. Add the Pexels 200/hour ceiling on the free-signup critical path with no fallback, and D1's unraisable 10 GB cap against a schema that writes a full page tree per regeneration, and you have five things that would each surface as a production incident. None of them touch the core architecture: fix the instance ID, pin effort, measure thinking, cache Pexels queries, and decide the D1 sharding story now — and this is a sound foundation to build Phase 1 on. Do not start writing code until the D1 decision is made, because that one is the only true one-way door in the document.
